subject: Basketry
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a practical paper. Two projects are set and the candidate executes one over five days at six hours a day, for 80 marks. The question paper arrives two weeks early, and the sketches and preparatory notes made in that time carry 20 marks, giving 100 marks in all.

practicals.title: Field survey and testing of basketry materials
practicals.aim: To collect, identify and classify local basketry materials and test how pliable they are.
apparatus: Rods or dowels 2 cm in diameter (for the bending test)
materials: Samples of raffia, rattan or cane, palm frond strips, bamboo, sisal, grass, banana fibre and plastic strapping
safety: Wear long sleeves and gloves, because palm and cane have spines.
Watch for snakes and insects in the bush.
Use the cutlass carefully.
Collect only with permission and do not strip whole plants.
procedure: Visit a nearby bush, farm or market and collect labelled samples of each material.
Record the plant source, the part used, the colour, the length and the texture.
Classify each material as natural or synthetic, and as flexible (pliable) or stiff (rigid).
Bending test: soak 12 cane strips of the same size for 30 minutes, bend each round the 2 cm rod, and count how many crack.
Repeat the bending test with dry strips and compare.
Present the results in a table with sketches or photos.
practicals.expectedObservations: Raffia, grass and soaked cane bend easily. Dry cane and bamboo are rigid and crack when bent sharply. Synthetic strapping is uniform and does not rot.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Bending test: 3 out of 12 soaked strips cracked, so 3 / 12 x 100 = 25% cracked and 75% passed. If 9 of 12 dry strips cracked, that is 75%, which shows that soaking improves pliability.
precautions: Use strips of the same size for a fair test.
Soak all the strips for the same time.
commonMistakes: Not stating the plant part used (leaf, stem, bark).
Mixing up raffia with sisal.
examTips: Classify the materials correctly and give their uses.
Mention conservation: harvest sustainably and replant.

practicals.title: Preparing, dyeing and storing materials
practicals.aim: To clean, split, soak, dry, dye and store raffia and cane ready for use.
materials: Acid or basic dye, or a natural dye (for example camwood)
Salt or vinegar (as the dye instructions require)
Insect-repellent leaves or a mild preservative
safety: Split away from your body.
Handle hot dye with gloves.
Store preservatives safely and label them.
procedure: Strip the raffia from the frond and split it to an even width. Scrape the cane to remove the glossy skin where needed.
Soak the cane in water (about 30 minutes for thin cane) until it is pliable.
Weigh the dry raffia and calculate the water and dye needed.
Dissolve the dye, wet the raffia, and simmer it in the dye bath for 30 to 45 minutes, stirring.
Rinse, then dry in the shade so that the colour does not fade.
Tie the material into hanks and store it in a dry, ventilated place, protected from insects and mould.
practicals.expectedObservations: Evenly split strands weave more neatly. Dried raffia stays bright when shade-dried. Damp storage leads to mould and rot.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For 500 g of raffia at a liquor ratio of 1:30, water = 500 x 30 = 15,000 g, about 15 litres. Dye at 3% = 0.03 x 500 = 15 g. For 200 g of raffia: water 6 litres and dye 6 g.
precautions: Keep the raffia under the dye liquor.
commonMistakes: Drying dyed raffia in strong sun, which fades it.
Storing damp hanks, which go mouldy.
examTips: Describe both chemical and non-chemical methods of preservation.
Mention protecting material sources by avoiding bush burning.

practicals.title: Drawing, improvising and caring for basketry tools
practicals.aim: To draw and label the common basketry tools to scale, and improvise a bodkin and a gauge from local materials.
materials: An old bicycle spoke or a large nail
safety: Keep blades closed or sheathed when not in use.
File improvised points smooth on the shank so that only the tip is sharp.
procedure: Lay out the tools and identify each one and its use: cutting, piercing and opening spaces, packing the weave down, measuring, shaping.
Measure each tool and draw it at a scale of 1:2, labelled.
Improvise a bodkin: file a bicycle spoke to a tapered point and set it in a wooden handle.
Make a gauge for strip width from a notched piece of hardwood.
Clean, oil and store all the tools after use.
practicals.expectedObservations: Improvised tools work well if they are smooth and well shaped. Rusty or blunt tools tear the materials.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A knife 24 cm long drawn at 1:2 measures 24 / 2 = 12 cm. A bodkin 18 cm long drawn at 1:2 measures 9 cm. A rapping iron drawn 13 cm long at 1:2 is 26 cm in real life.
sourcesOfError: Measuring curved tools along a straight line.
commonMistakes: Drawing without a scale.
Confusing a bodkin (for piercing) with a rapping iron (for packing).
examTips: Learn the name and use of each tool.
State safety and maintenance practices.

practicals.title: Coiling a raffia and grass basket
practicals.aim: To make a coiled basket with a flat base 20 cm in diameter and straight sides, using grass bundles stitched with raffia.
apparatus: Gauge ring (a 1 cm bottle neck or tube)
materials: Raffia for wrapping and stitching (natural and dyed)
safety: Keep needles in a pin cushion.
Grass edges can cut, so handle them carefully.
procedure: Taper the end of a grass bundle, wrap it tightly with raffia for 3 cm, and coil it into a tight centre.
Stitch each new round to the previous one (lazy squaw or Navajo stitch), keeping the bundle 1 cm thick by feeding it through the gauge.
Add grass to the core as it thins, and splice in new raffia under the wrapping.
At 20 cm diameter, start the sides by placing the coil on top of the previous round.
Space the stitches evenly. Add a colour pattern by changing to dyed raffia.
Finish by tapering the core and stitching it down neatly to form the rim.
practicals.expectedObservations: An even core gives a flat, regular spiral. Uneven feeding makes bumps, and tight stitching makes the base cup up.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A flat base 20 cm across (radius 10 cm) with a 1 cm coil needs 10 rounds. Their mean diameters are 1, 3, 5 ... 19 cm, which add up to 100 cm. Core length is about pi x 100 = 314 cm (3.14 m). Each 4 cm of side height adds 4 rounds of pi x 20 = 62.8 cm, so 251 cm more.
commonMistakes: Pulling stitches too tight on the base.
Splices that show on the surface.
examTips: Name the coiling stitches and show them in sketches.
Neat, regular stitching and a firm rim earn finishing marks.

practicals.title: Stake-and-strand (randing) cane basket
practicals.topic: Designing Articles to Suit Specific Needs
practicals.aim: To weave a round cane basket for holding fruit, with a woven base, upsett, randed sides and a trac border.
materials: Thick cane for the base sticks and side stakes
safety: Cut cane ends at an angle, away from your face.
Mind the springy cane ends near your eyes.
procedure: Plan a basket 20 cm across and 15 cm high. Cut and soak the stakes.
Make the base: cross two groups of 4 sticks (8 in total), tie them in with pairing, then open them out into spokes and pair to 20 cm diameter.
Insert two side stakes beside each base stick with the bodkin (16 stakes), then add one extra so the number is odd for single-weaver randing (17).
Upsett: bend the stakes up and weave 3 rounds of waling to set the shape.
Rand (in-and-out weaving with one weaver) up the sides, rapping down often to keep the height even.
Finish with a trac border (each stake goes behind and in front of the next stakes), then trim the ends.
practicals.expectedObservations: With an odd number of stakes a single weaver alternates automatically. With an even number it repeats the same path. The waling upsett gives firm, upright sides.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Stake length = base diameter + 2 x side height + 2 x border allowance = 20 + 2 x 15 + 2 x 12 = 74 cm. With 17 stakes cut separately, each from the edge of the base to the border, each stake = 10 (radius) + 15 + 12 = 37 cm, so the total is 17 x 37 = 629 cm of thick cane.
precautions: Keep the cane damp while working.
Rap down regularly so the sides are level.
sourcesOfError: Cane drying and shrinking after weaving.
commonMistakes: Using an even number of stakes with a single weaver.
Weaving too tight, which pulls the sides inward.
examTips: Show the stake calculation in your preparatory notes.
Name the weaves: randing, pairing, waling. Name the border type.

checkQuestions.explanation: An odd number lets the weave alternate.

checkQuestions.explanation: The upsett turns the stakes upward.

practicals.title: Plaiting a checked palm or raffia mat
practicals.aim: To plait a 60 cm x 40 cm table mat in a check (one over, one under) pattern with a bound edge.
materials: Prepared palm or raffia strips 2 cm wide (natural and dyed)
safety: Handle the knife carefully.
Palm edges are sharp.
procedure: Cut the strips: 30 strips of 50 cm (for the width direction) and 20 strips of 70 cm (for the length direction), including 10 cm turning allowance.
Lay the 30 strips side by side and clip them to the board.
Weave the 20 cross strips one at a time, over one and under one, alternating the starting point on each strip.
Push the strips close together to keep the check square.
Fold the ends back and tuck them under the adjacent strips, or bind the edge with raffia.
Press under a weight overnight to flatten.
practicals.expectedObservations: Alternating natural and dyed strips gives a chequerboard. Strips that are not pushed close leave gaps.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mat 60 x 40 cm with 2 cm strips: 60 / 2 = 30 strips crossing 40 / 2 = 20 strips. Lengths: 30 strips of 40 + 10 = 50 cm (1,500 cm) and 20 strips of 60 + 10 = 70 cm (1,400 cm). Total strip length = 2,900 cm, which is 29 m.
precautions: Cut the strips to an even width.
Keep the strips damp if they are brittle.
commonMistakes: Starting each cross strip in the same position, which leaves floats.
Forgetting the turning allowance.
examTips: Diagonal and check plaits are both accepted; name the one used.
Neat, flat finishing and edges score marks.

practicals.title: Macramé plant hanger with beads and cowries
practicals.aim: To make a macramé hanger using square knots, half-hitches and spiral knots, combined with beads or cowries.
apparatus: Clipboard or nail on a board
safety: Hold scissors carefully.
Mount the hook securely.
procedure: Cut 8 cords, each 4 times the finished length, then double it because each cord is folded in half over the ring.
Fold the cords over the ring and secure them with a gathering knot.
Divide the cords into four groups of four and tie square knots for 15 cm, adding beads on the middle cords.
Join neighbouring groups with alternating square knots to make the net that holds the pot.
Gather all the cords with a wrapping knot, attach cowries, and trim the tassel.
Test with a pot and adjust.
practicals.expectedObservations: Square knots lie flat, while half-knots tied repeatedly twist into a spiral. Knotting uses a lot of cord.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: For a finished length of 60 cm: each cord = 4 x 60 = 240 cm, doubled for folding = 480 cm. Eight cords need 8 x 480 = 3,840 cm, which is 38.4 m. At N150 per metre that costs 38.4 x 150 = N5,760.
precautions: Keep the groups the same length.
commonMistakes: Cutting the cords too short.
Confusing the left and right half of a square knot, which gives a spiral by accident.
examTips: Sketch each knot with labels.
Show the cord calculation.

practicals.title: Frame work: a cane-lashed stool
practicals.aim: To build a rigid frame of bamboo or thick rattan, lash the joints with cane, and weave a seat.
materials: Weaving cane or seagrass for the seat
safety: Clamp the work for sawing.
Heat rods and bending fires need supervision.
Wear gloves.
procedure: Draw a working drawing: seat 40 cm x 40 cm, height 45 cm.
Cut 4 legs of 45 cm and 8 rails of 40 cm.
Mark and cut the joints, drill pilot holes, and peg the rails to the legs at the top and at a lower level.
Check that the frame is square and level.
Lash each joint tightly with wet binding cane in a cross pattern, tucking the ends in.
Weave the seat across the top rails in a check or herringbone pattern.
Trim, sand and varnish.
practicals.expectedObservations: Wet lashing shrinks as it dries and tightens the joints. A frame that is not square rocks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Poles: legs 4 x 45 = 180 cm and rails 8 x 40 = 320 cm, so 500 cm in all. With 10% allowance for joints and waste, 500 x 1.1 = 550 cm (5.5 m) of pole. Seat: 40 cm wide with a 1 cm strand spacing needs 40 / 1 = 40 strands in each direction.
precautions: Check that the frame is square before lashing.
Pre-drill so the bamboo does not split.
commonMistakes: Lashing dry cane, which goes slack.
Uneven leg lengths.
examTips: Working drawings with a materials list earn marks.
Comment on function, strength and finish.

practicals.title: Elements of design in raffia: dot, line, texture and the colour wheel
practicals.aim: To make a sampler that shows the elements of design through basketry techniques, and a 12-part colour wheel of dyed raffia.
materials: Raffia dyed in primary, secondary and tertiary colours
safety: Use the compass point carefully.
procedure: Draw a circle 16 cm across on card and divide it into 12 equal sectors.
Fill the primary sectors (red, yellow, blue), then the secondaries (orange, green, violet) between them, then the six tertiaries, using wrapped or glued raffia.
On a sampler, show a dot (a bead or a knot), lines (wrapping or a stitched line), shapes (woven motifs) and texture (waling against randing).
Label each element and each technique used.
practicals.expectedObservations: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the wheel (for example red and green). Different weaves give clearly different textures.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Each sector of a 12-part wheel = 360 / 12 = 30 degrees. Complementary colours are 6 sectors apart = 180 degrees. Analogous colours are neighbouring sectors, 30 degrees apart.
precautions: Keep the colours in the correct order.
sourcesOfError: Dyed colours differ from the theoretical hues.
commonMistakes: Putting secondary colours next to the wrong primaries.
Leaving the elements unlabelled.
examTips: Relate each element to a basketry technique, for example a knot or bead for a dot and waling for texture.
Know the primary, secondary, tertiary and complementary colours.

practicals.title: Applying principles of design: a repeat-pattern border
practicals.aim: To plan and weave a border pattern that shows repetition, balance and rhythm.
apparatus: Small frame or the side of a basket
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Design a 4.5 cm motif on graph paper.
Plan how it repeats round a 36 cm band, using symmetrical balance and rhythm by alternating colours.
Transfer the plan into the weave by changing colours at the marked stakes.
Evaluate the result for unity, balance and proportion.
practicals.expectedObservations: An exact repeat gives rhythm and unity. A motif that does not divide the band leaves an awkward part-motif.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Number of repeats = 36 / 4.5 = 8. If the stakes are 1.5 cm apart, each motif spans 4.5 / 1.5 = 3 stakes, and the band needs 36 / 1.5 = 24 stakes. That is an even number, so use pairing or add one stake for single-weaver randing.
precautions: Plan the repeats to divide the band exactly.
commonMistakes: A part-motif at the join.
Too many colours, which lose unity.
examTips: Name the principles (balance, rhythm, repetition, proportion, unity, contrast) and show where each appears.

practicals.title: Design brief, sketches and working drawing for a basketry article
practicals.aim: To develop a design for a functional basketry article from a brief, using observation, memory and imagination, and to produce scaled working drawings.
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Analyse the brief: user, function, size, materials and cost limit.
Draw at least three idea sketches from observation (local baskets), memory and imagination.
Choose one idea and give reasons.
Draw the elevation and plan to scale with dimensions, and show the technique and the colour plan.
List the materials with quantities, the tools, and the steps. Make a day-by-day plan for the five days.
practicals.expectedObservations: A clear working drawing makes the later material calculations and making accurate.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A shopping basket 40 cm long x 25 cm wide x 30 cm high drawn at 1:5 measures 8 cm x 5 cm x 6 cm. Its rim perimeter (as a rectangle) = 2 x (40 + 25) = 130 cm. With stakes 2 cm apart that needs 130 / 2 = 65 stakes.
precautions: Check that the design meets every requirement of the brief.
commonMistakes: Ignoring function, for example no handle on a shopping basket.
No material list.
examTips: Sketches and preparatory notes carry 20 marks. Show the development of ideas.

practicals.title: Decoration and finishing: scorching, spraying, borders and varnishing
practicals.aim: To decorate and finish a woven basket by scorching or spraying, then trim, singe, bind the rim and varnish it.
apparatus: Blow lamp or candle (for scorching and singeing, with supervision)
safety: Scorching and singeing use flame. Work outdoors, away from loose fibres, and keep water nearby.
Spray and varnish only in a ventilated area and wear a mask.
Keep flames away from varnish and solvents.
procedure: Trim the projecting ends flush, and singe off fluffy fibres with a quick pass of the flame.
Scorch the chosen areas lightly for brown tones, or mask and spray a colour pattern.
Bind or wrap the rim with cane or raffia to make a neat, strong border.
Sand any rough areas lightly.
Apply the first coat of varnish thinly, inside and out. Let it dry, then apply a second coat.
practicals.expectedObservations: Thin coats dry clear. Thick coats run and stay tacky. Scorching gives graded tones, but overheating burns through.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Cylindrical basket 30 cm across and 25 cm high: side area = pi x 30 x 25 = 2,356.19 cm2 and base area = pi x 15 x 15 = 706.86 cm2, total 3,063.05 cm2. Inside and outside = 6,126 cm2 = 0.613 m2. Two coats need 1.225 m2 of coverage. With varnish covering 10 m2 per litre: 1.225 / 10 = 0.1225 L, about 125 ml.
precautions: Let each coat dry before applying the next.
sourcesOfError: Woven surfaces absorb more varnish than the flat-area estimate.
commonMistakes: Singeing too long, which burns the strands.
Varnishing a dusty basket.
examTips: List the finishing processes by name.
A clean, even finish strongly affects the general impression mark.

practicals.title: Costing and pricing baskets: fixed cost, variable cost and profit
practicals.aim: To work out the full cost, unit cost, selling price and profit for a batch of baskets.
materials: Material receipts and records of workshop costs
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Separate the variable costs (materials, packaging, labour per item) from the fixed costs (rent, tool wear, per month).
Share the monthly fixed cost across the expected output.
Add up the batch costs and divide by the number of baskets.
Apply the markup, then check the price against competitors and against plastic substitutes.
practicals.expectedObservations: Making more items each month spreads the fixed costs and lowers the unit cost.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Batch of 10 baskets. Variable: raffia 2 kg x N2,500 = N5,000, dye N1,500, cane N3,000, varnish N2,000, packaging 10 x N150 = N1,500, total N13,000. Labour 10 x N600 = N6,000. Fixed costs are N12,000 a month for 24 baskets, so this batch's share = 12,000 x 10 / 24 = N5,000. Total = 13,000 + 6,000 + 5,000 = N24,000. Unit cost = N2,400. At 25% markup the price is N3,000 and the profit per batch is N6,000.
precautions: Review prices as material costs change.
sourcesOfError: Estimated output differs from actual output.
commonMistakes: Charging the whole month's fixed cost to one batch.
Ignoring labour.
examTips: Define variable cost, fixed cost and profit with examples.
State the factors that determine price: cost, demand, competition, quality.
